<reason>Side A won a closely fought, well-matched debate. A's core strategy — showing that every time B made "safety" concrete it became an enforceable right (appeal in B's own baseline, non-splitting, then subsistence in B4.1) — steadily eroded B's graded standard, and A's closing (A5.1) converted B's "bargaining chip" jab (B4.4) into a PRO win: if the three rights are cheap to legislate, refusing them reveals the transfer as disposal, and the "only" test forces improvement ("negotiate the ban away") rather than cruelty. B landed real damage: the subsistence-vs-work distinction (B4.1) and the act-vs-entitlement distinction on family (B2.5/B4.3) successfully limited A's collapse narrative, and the comparative-alternatives frame was never fully dissolved. But B's live route — that A's rule strands refugees with crueler outcomes — was answered by the no-floor principle plus the cheap-compliance alternative, which B's closing only restated rather than repaired. B also bore a heavier execution cost, with five turns clipped for length (opening, both rebuttals' ends, closing) versus one for A, losing the tail of B's closing argument mid-sentence.</best_rebuttal>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive sequence ran from B4.4 ("safety that can be legislated overnight was never the line") through A5.1, where A reversed it: a bar a state can meet almost for free means refusal is a confession that the deal was disposal, not protection — turning B's own concession into the closing reason to vote PRO.</best_rebuttal>
